meta.title: Penalties deep dive, 2026 SWAC
meta.scope: SWAC vs SWAC games; accepted flags unless stated
meta.keys: team_id / player_id / game_path_id match the site's other files; the frontend owns team display names

net_penalty_battle.definition: Per game in games against SWAC opponents: accepted penalty yards (and flags) on the team's opponents, on the team, and the difference (opponents minus team). Garbage time included.

all_18_without_garbage_time.definition: Net penalty yards per game in all games between two of the 18 programs, with and without garbage-time plays.

officiating_crews.definition: A crew is a group of officials who work games together: SWAC games that share 3 or more officials belong to the same crew. Core officials worked a majority of the crew's games. ratio_to_swac = the crew's per-game count of a foul / the SWAC per-game count (fouls the crew called 4+ times; listed at 1.3+ or 0.7 and below).

cost_by_foul.definition: Accepted flags by foul. epa_given = expected points the flagged team lost on flags that wiped out the snap. auto_first_downs_given = flags that gave the other team a first down. first_downs_erased = offensive flags that wiped out a play that had gained a first down. crucial and decisive as defined under team_cost.

team_cost.definition: Per team, its own accepted flags. crucial = a flag on 3rd or 4th down, in the red zone, on goal-to-go or in the two-minute drill, with the game within 8 points, outside garbage time. decisive = a defensive flag that gave an automatic first down on a drive that went on to score at least the final margin for the team that won.

game_swinging_flags.definition: win_probability_change = the change in the flagged team's win probability on a flag that wiped out the snap (0.24 = 24 points); empty when the play stood, because the change then belongs mostly to the play. Largest 15 drops among wiped snaps, and every decisive flag.

bounce_back.definition: After an accepted offensive flag on its own drive, whether the offense still gained a first down or scored before the drive ended. normal_rate = the same from that down and distance when no offensive flag came before it (null where that situation almost only follows a flag).

third_down_flags.definition: Accepted flags on 3rd down. Offense: the team's own flags on its drive, whether that series still moved the chains, whether the drive scored. Defense: flags on the team's defense, whether the opponent's series continued, whether that drive scored.

habits_and_direction.definition: Accepted flags per game in date order. flags_spread = standard deviation across games. first/second half = the first and last half of the team's games (the middle game of five is in neither). direction = 'fewer' or 'more' when the halves differ by 2+ flags a game and the per-game change agrees (0.75+ a game); otherwise null. most_common_foul = the foul with the most accepted flags (ties: called in more games); most_common_foul_flags = its count; most_common_foul_games = in how many of the team's games it was called.

flags_and_winning.definition: In each game, the team better on a measure vs the team that won. Games where both teams are level on the measure are left out. one_score = games decided by 8 or fewer.

when.definition: Accepted flags. phase: pre_snap (before the snap), live (during the play), dead (after the whistle: unsportsmanlike conduct, sideline, disqualification, equipment). side: the flagged team's unit (a flag on a kick play is special_teams).

who.definition: Accepted flags that name a player (position from the 2026 roster). The play-by-play charges delay of game to the quarterback.

findings.text: Southern's opponents are penalized 20.6 more yards a game than Southern in SWAC games, the most in the conference; MVSU is −26.2, the least.
The Pinkard crew (the same seven officials in all five of its games) called 7 flags in one game and 31 in another (PVAMU at MVSU).
The Green, Spears, Pinchback, King and Harris crew called 17, 18, 16 and 21 flags; it calls block in the back 3.7×, unsportsmanlike conduct 2.4× and facemask 2.0× the SWAC rate.
The Daniels crew calls pass interference 1.8× and holding 0.4× the SWAC rate; 53% of its flags are on defenses.
The Quinn / McCants crew worked four games with two different referees: Jarvis Walker (3) and Kenith Garmond (1).
Home teams drew more flags than visitors from the Green crew (44–28), the Myers crew (39–26) and the Daniels crew (26–14).
Pass interference cost SWAC teams 81 expected points and 41 automatic first downs, the most of any foul.
Holding is the most-called foul (91) and erased 12 first downs.
Roughing the passer costs the most per flag: 1.8 expected points.
44% of UAPB's flags came in crucial situations, the highest share in the SWAC.
JSU's pass interference at Grambling with 2:00 left cost JSU 24 points of win probability, the largest single-flag swing in SWAC play. JSU had three decisive flags in that 45–38 loss.
TSU's pass interference wiped out an interception on Southern's 4th & 4 and cost TSU 21 points of win probability.
AAMU had three drive-extending fouls in its 31–28 loss at JSU: a personal foul, targeting and pass interference.
PVAMU's roughing the holder on 3rd & 19 at MVSU kept alive a touchdown drive in a game PVAMU lost 28–27.
AAMU's offense still moved the chains or scored after 10 of its 12 offensive flags (83%), the best in the SWAC.
ASU recovered after 1 of its 7 offensive flags; Southern after 4 of 12.
After a flag, offenses facing 3rd & 16 or longer converted 23% of the time (31% when no flag got them there).
Offenses still converted 61% of series after a false start, 52% after holding.
Defensive flags on 3rd down gave the offense a first down 30 of 36 times.
MVSU's defense was flagged 6 times on 3rd down: 5 first downs, 3 scoring drives. B-CU's went 4 for 4.
MVSU's offense had 8 flags on 3rd down and continued the series once; PVAMU 0 of 4; JSU 0 of 4.
Alcorn continued the series after 3 of its 4 third-down offensive flags, and all three drives scored.
TSU's pre-snap flags fell from 16 in the first half of its games to 5 in the second.
MVSU's flags by game: 10, 15, 14, 15.
AAMU's pre-snap flags rose from 3 to 6; B-CU's from 1 to 5.
TSU, Grambling and Alcorn were called for a false start in every game; PVAMU, MVSU, UAPB and B-CU for holding; AAMU and B-CU for pass interference.
The team with fewer flags won 13 of 25 SWAC games; the team that lost less EPA to flags won 15 of 26.
The 2nd quarter draws the most flags (129). In the red zone, 33 of 58 flags come before the snap; in the two-minute drill, 26 of 37 come during the play.
Offensive linemen draw the most flags (69: 35 false starts, 22 holding); defensive backs are next (64, 34 of them pass interference).

tidbits.text: TSU's drop in pre-snap fouls (16 to 5) is the clearest sign of discipline being coached. Pre-snap fouls are the ones a team controls entirely.
Watch Alcorn: its total is flat (9, 13, 13, 9 flags), but its pre-snap fouls are rising (8 to 12).
AAMU is still one of the cleanest teams in the SWAC (7.0 flags a game, 5th fewest), but its flags (9 in its latest game) and pre-snap fouls (3 to 6) are both creeping up.
PVAMU's spiky label is mostly one game: without its 16-flag game it is a 4-to-8-flag team.
AAMU and B-CU are disciplined overall, but both were called for pass interference in every game (AAMU's most common foul) -- the same foul behind 10 of the 22 decisive flags.
AAMU's flags are rare but land at bad moments: its offense's flags erased 4 first downs, tied for the most in the SWAC.
UAPB (44%) and B-CU (38%) are rarely flagged, but a big share of their flags come at crucial moments. That is the 'fix this' story, more than a raw count.
AAMU's offense shrugs off its own flags better than anyone in the SWAC (10 of 12 series saved).
ASU commits the fewest offensive flags (7) and Southern the fewest flags overall (4.6 a game) -- but when they are flagged on offense, the drive rarely survives (ASU 1 of 7, Southern 4 of 12).
A false start isn't fatal: offenses still convert 61% of those series. Holding hurts more (52%).
On defense, a 3rd-down flag almost always hands over the series (30 of 36). On offense, it usually ends the drive -- except at Alcorn, where 3 of 4 still scored.
The same seven officials can call 7 flags one week and 31 the next, while another crew calls 16 to 21 every week.
No sign of home cooking: home teams draw more flags than visitors from the Green, Myers and Daniels crews.
Near the goal line, teams beat themselves before the snap: 33 of 58 red-zone flags are pre-snap.
Counting flags is a coin flip for picking the winner. What the flags cost leans toward winning.
